newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Socialists, Democrats in last Albania poll rallies.
newsitem.headline: Socialists, Democrats in last Albania poll rallies.

text.p: President Sali Berisha's ruling Democratic Party and the Socialists challenging them for power held final rallies on Friday in Albania's hard-fought election, each pledging to deliver the country from violence.

Hundreds of armed police surrounded Tirana's Skanderbeg Square as Socialist Party chairman Fatos Nano promised a crowd of more than 5,000 he would end months of lawlessness triggered off by the crash of a string of shady investment funds.

"Albania needs peace and calm. It needs the smiles of everybody, especially the children, mothers and sisters. No dictator will take that smile away any more," Nano said. "We will bring you joy, hope and the future."
Berisha, who blames the Socialists for unrest, was due to address a rally in the same place at around 7 p.m. (1700 GMT).
The election on Sunday is widely viewed as the last means of establishing order seven years after the fall of one of eastern Europe's most repressive communist regimes.
Some 450 observers have been dispatched to oversee the vote and a 7,000-strong multinational protection force will help keep polling stations safe.
U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright, in a message read on the Voice of America, urged Albanians to turn out to vote "to chart a better future for your country".

"I too have experienced times of political and economic uncertainty," Albright, born in pre-war Czechoslovakia, said. "The gesture of voting is a very important one for me, for I have witnessed societies where this right was not allowed."

On the last feverish day of campaigning, Berisha told a gathering in the northern city of Shkoder that his Democrats would score "a triumph over terror and communist rebellion which have terrorised southern regions for four months".
The official ATA news agency said he repeated his pledge to restore peace to the country of 3.4 million within 75 days.

Democratic Party secretary-general Genc Pollo told a news conference his party and allied parties would win around 50 percent of the vote but were also prepared to become the official opposition in the event of a leftist victory.

The rallies mark the end of an electoral campaign waged against the backdrop of increasing anarchy and violence, particularly in the south of the poverty-stricken nation, which remains largely outside government control.

At least eight people were wounded on Thursday night when shooting erupted during an address by Berisha to supporters in Lushnje, about 80 km (50 miles) south of Tirana. The Democrats later blamed leftist extremists for opening fire on the crowd.

The Democrats have found it practically impossible to campaign in the south, accusing Nano's Socialists, reformed successors of the communists, of using armed gangs to incite violence in a desperate effort to win Sunday's polls.
Nano, 45, blames the unrest on the Democrats and claims the Socialists would strive to reimburse investors for their losses, estimated at some $1.2 billion.
Berisha called the early election as part of a pact struck at the height of the disturbances in March to set up an interim unity government made up of 10 parties.

The vote is being held 13 months after Albania's third multi-party elections since the collapse of communism in 1990. International observers said the 1996 vote was subject to manipulation and voter intimidation.

The Democrats won 122 of the 140 parliamentary seats then. Berisha, a former heart surgeon, maintained the vote was held correctly and steadfastly ignored demands from Washington and some European states to rerun it.
But when a number of high-risk pyramid investment schemes collapsed early this year, the government's grip on power began to weaken.
